newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan urges China to prevent illegal immigration.
newsitem.headline: Japan urges China to prevent illegal immigration.

text.p: Japan, alarmed at an increasing number of attempts by Chinese nationals to sneak into the country, urged China on Thursday to step up measures to prevent further illegal immigration.

Japan"s Foreign Ministry formally asked Beijing to step up patrols along Chinese coastlines and to crack down on Chinese brokers profiting from the smuggling trade, the ministry said in a written statement.
The request follows a recent rise in the number of Chinese nationals trying to enter Japan illegally.
In the past two months alone Japan took 330 Chinese nationals into custody for attempting to enter Japan illegally, government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama said on Thursday.
"Those are just the cases discovered. Those not discovered are another problem," Kajiyama told a news conference.

The Chinese entering Japan illegally "are turning into a major social problem in Japan and could influence Sino-Japanese relations if this continues", Ryozo Kato, the head of the Foreign Ministry"s Asia Division, was quoted by ministry officials as telling a Chinese embassy official in Tokyo.

Last year, police reported a record 29 cases of illegal entry in groups. Of the 679 people taken into custody, 545 were identified as Chinese, according to National Police Agency statistics. In 1995, 151 of 324 were identified as Chinese.
Japan"s concern has been amplified by an increasing number of arrests of Chinese nationals for carjackings, robbery and even murder.
On Thursday, Japanese police indicted six Chinese men on suspicion of kidnapping four compatriots last week and demanding 35 million yen ($282,000) in ransom.
Chinese "Snakehead" brokers and Japanese gangsters are believed to be involved in bringing in the illegals, who mainly come from the southern Chinese province of Fujian.

In a problem that the United States began grappling with several years ago, the illegal immigrants usually borrow the broking fee, sometimes worth their lifetime"s earnings, from relatives and the brokers.

Some successfully find jobs and return home after several years, but others who fail to repay the swelling debt are imprisoned by the Snakeheads and forced to engage in criminal activities, Japanese media reports say.
According to police statistics, Chinese nationals accounted for more than 35 percent of the 13,000 recorded criminal cases in Japan involving foreigners between January and October last year.
Those caught by police constantly refer to Snakeheads, professional Chinese brokers feared for their snake-like viciousness, as being behind the trade in human capital.
Police declined to comment on the issue.

The Tokyo Metropolitan Police Department set up a special investigation squad last month to track down the brokers, but admit they are nowhere close to identifying the core of the mysterious group rumoured to be headed by the Chinese mafia, media reports said.
Police also suspect that some 1,000 members of groups affiliated with Hong Kong"s "14K" (14 karat) crime syndicate to be active in Japan, Japan"s Asahi Shimbun reported on Thursday.

Their activities in Japan range from theft and smuggling of drugs and guns to counterfeiting and arranging marriages of convenience between Japanese and foreigners who want to immigrate to Japan, Asahi said. ($1=124 yen)
